Opponent-process theory for color vision.Definition: Proposed mechanism for color vision with opposing retinal processes for red–green, yellow–blue, white–black. Some retinal cells are stimulated by one of a pair and inhibited by the other.

Opponent-process theory of emotions.Definition: Following a strong emotion, an opposing emotion counters the first emotion lessening the experience of that emotion. On repeated occasions, the opposing emotion becomes stronger.

Optic nerve.Definition: Nerve formed by ganglion cell axons; carries the neural impulses from the eye to the thalamus of the brain.

Optical or visual illusions.Definition: Discrepancies between the appearance of a visual stimulus and its physical reality.

Oral stage.Definition: Freud's first psychosexual stage; pleasure is derived from sucking. Crisis is weaning from bottle or breast fixation: oral-dependent personalities who are gullible, overeaters, or talkative and oral-aggressives who are argumentative or sarcastic.

Organismic self.Definition: According to Rogers, the original (real) self that strives toward positive goals until it is influenced by society.

Out-group.Definition: Groups to which we do not belong.

Out-group homogeneity.Definition: Belief that members of another group are more similar in their attitudes than they really are.

Ovaries.Definition: Gonads in females that produce hormones necessary for reproduction and development of secondary sex characteristics.

Overconfidence bias.Definition: The tendency to overestimate the accuracy of our beliefs and judgments that can hinder problem solving.

Overgeneralization or overregularization.Definition: Application of grammatical rules without making appropriate exceptions.

Overjustification effect.Definition: Where getting a reward for doing something we already like to do results in our seeing the reward as the motivation for performing the task. When the reward is taken away, the behavior tends to disappear.

Pancreas.Definition: Gland near stomach that secretes the hormones insulin and glucagon that regulates blood sugar necessary for fueling all behavioral processes. Imbalances result in diabetes and hypoglycemia.

Panic disorder.Definition: Unpredictable attacks of acute anxiety accompanied by high levels of physiological arousal that last from a few seconds to a few hours.

Parallel distributive processing (PDP).Definition: Performing several operations simultaneously as opposed to serially or one operation after another. Parallel processing—to simultaneously analyze different elements of sensory information such as color, shape, brightness, etc.

Paranoid personality disorder.Definition: Symptoms include delusions of persecution that are generally organized around one theme.

Paranoid schizophrenia.Definition: A form of schizophrenia in which the person suffers from delusions of persecution, grandeur, reference, or control.

Parapsychology.Definition: Study of paranormal events that investigates claims of ESP, including telepathy, clairvoyance, precognition, and telekinesis or psychokinesis.

Parasympathetic nervous system.Definition: Subdivision of PNS and ANS whose stimulation calms your body following sympathetic stimulation by restoring normal body processes.

Parathyroids.Definition: Endocrine glands in neck that produce parathyroid hormone that helps maintain calcium ion level in blood necessary for normal functioning of neurons.

Parietal lobes.Definition: Region on the top of the cerebral cortex the front strip of which is the somatosensory cortex that processes sensory information including touch, temperature, and pain from body parts; association areas perceive objects.

Peg word mnemonic.Definition: Memory device that uses a scheme (“One is a bun, two is . . .”) we memorize, then associate with names or objects in a series.

Percentile score.Definition: The percentage of scores at or below a particular score, from 1 to 99.

Perception.Definition: The process of selecting, organizing, and interpreting sensations, enabling you to recognize meaningful objects and events.

Perceptual constancy.Definition: Perceiving an object as unchanging even when the immediate sensation of the object changes.

Peripheral nervous system (PNS).Definition: Portion of the nervous system outside the brain and spinal cord. It includes all of the sensory and motor neurons, and subdivisions called the autonomic and somatic nervous systems.

Peripheral route of persuasion.Definition: Changes attitudes by pairing superficial positive stimuli (supermodels and celebrities) with an argument; leads to unstable change in attitudes.

Permissive parenting style.Definition: Parents set no firm guidelines for behavior and tend to give in to demands of the child.

Persona.Definition: According to Jung, this is the outward part of the personality or the mask we wear when dealing with society and opposite of the unconscious shadow.

Personal constructs.Definition: A set of bipolar categories we use as labels to help us categorize and interpret the world; Kelly believes that personality is a habitual way we live our lives trying to make sense out of what happens.

Personal fable.Definition: Exaggerated belief in a person's uniqueness and immortality in adolescence.

Personal unconscious.Definition: According to Jung, a storehouse of all our past memories and hidden instincts and urges unique to the individual.

Personality.Definition: A unique pattern of consistent feelings, thoughts, and behaviors that originate within the individual.

Personality disorders.Definition: Chronic, maladaptive thought and behavior patterns that are troublesome to others, harmful, or illegal.

Phallic stage.Definition: Freud's third stage of psychosexual development; the primary erogenous zone is the genital area; during this time children become attached to the opposite-sex parent.

Phenylketonuria (PKU).Definition: Recessive trait that results in severe, irreversible brain damage unless the baby is fed a special diet low in phenylalanine.

Phobia.Definition: Irrational fear of specific objects or situations, such as animals or enclosed spaces.

Phonemes.Definition: Smallest possible sound units of spoken language.

Photoreceptors.Definition: Modified neurons (rods and cones) that convert light energy to electrochemical neural impulses at the retina.

Physiological motivations.Definition: Such as hunger, thirst, and sex. Each is influenced by biological factors, environmental factors and learned preferences and habits. The hypothalamus and endocrine system are implicated in each of these motives.

Pineal gland.Definition: Endocrine gland in brain that produces melatonin that helps regulate circadian rhythms and is associated with seasonal affective disorder.

Pitch.Definition: The highness or lowness of a sound. The shorter the wavelength, the higher the frequency and pitch. The longer the wavelength, the lower the frequency and the lower the pitch.

Pituitary gland.Definition: Endocrine gland in brain that produces stimulating hormones which promote secretion by other glands, including TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone); ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone), which stimulates the adrenal cortex; FSH (follicle- stimulating hormone), which stimulates egg or sperm production; ADH (antidiuretic hormone), to help retain water in your body; and HGH (human growth hormone).

Place theory.Definition: The position on the basilar membrane at which waves reach their peak depending on the frequency of a tone. Accounts well for high- pitched sounds.

Placebo.Definition: A physical or psychological treatment given to the control group that resembles the treatment given to the experimental group but contains no active ingredient.

Placebo effect.Definition: A response to the belief that the independent variable will have an effect, rather than to the actual effect of the independent variable; can be a confounding variable.

Plasticity.Definition: Modifiability of neural connections that enables generation of new synapses which results in storing and retrieval of memories or one part of the brain taking over the function of another.

Pleasure principle.Definition: Freud's claim that the id part of the personality seeks immediate gratification of its wants and needs.

Pons.Definition: Part of brainstem that includes portion of reticular activating system or reticular formation critical for arousal and wakefulness; sends information to and from medulla, cerebellum, and cerebral cortex.

Population.Definition: All the individuals in the group to which the study applies.

Positive psychology.Definition: The scientific study of optimal human functioning.

Positive reinforcement.Definition: A rewarding consequence that follows a voluntary behavior, thereby increasing the probability the behavior will be repeated.

Positron emission tomography (PET).Definition: Shows brain activity when radioactively tagged glucose rushes to active neurons and emits positrons.

Postconventional level.Definition: Kohlberg's third and final level of moral development, in which people come to understand that moral rules include principles that apply across all situations and societies.

Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).Definition: Disorder in which the individual has feelings of social withdrawal accompanied by atypically low levels of emotion caused by prolonged exposure to a stressor, such as a catastrophe; may experience flashbacks and nightmares.

Power tests.Definition: Difficulty level measured; untimed tests which include easy to more difficult questions, used to assess intelligence and other capacities.

Preconscious.Definition: The level of consciousness that is outside of awareness but contains feelings and memories that can easily be brought to conscious awareness.

Preconventional level.Definition: Kohlberg's first level of moral development, which bases moral behavior on obedience and punishment or acting in one's own best interests.

Predictive validity.Definition: The extent to which a test accurately forecasts a specific future result.

Prefrontal lobotomy.Definition: A surgical procedure that destroys the tracts connecting the frontal lobes to lower centers of the brain, once believed to be an effective treatment for schizophrenia.

Prejudice.Definition: Unjustified attitudes we hold about others; generally negative evaluation based on ethnicity, race, sex, or some other criterion.

Prelinguistic speech.Definition: Initial steps of cooing and babbling, later accidental imitation, and finally deliberate imitation as precursors to language development.

Premack principle.Definition: A high probability behavior can serve as a reward for a low probability behavior, thus increasing it.

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder.Definition: A recurrent depressive disorder occurring most months in the days before a woman starts menstruating characterized by mood swings, feeling suddenly sad or tearful, irritability or anger, feelings of being “keyed up,” difficulty concentrating, lack of energy, change in appetite, change in sleep patterns, sensation of bloating.

Prenatal development.Definition: Period of development that begins with fertilization, or conception, and ends with birth.

Preoperational stage.Definition: Piaget's second stage of cognitive development (2– 7 years) during which the child represents and manipulates objects with symbols (language) and is egocentric.

Primacy effect (Law of Primacy).Definition: The tendency to remember initial information; in the memorization of a list of words, the primacy effect is evidenced by better recall of the words early in the list.

Primary emotions.Definition: Joy, fear, anger, sadness, surprise, and disgust, which are inborn.

Primary motives.Definition: Internal mechanism directing behavior dealing with sustaining processes biologically necessary for survival such as thirst, hunger, and sex.

Primary reinforcers.Definition: Important automatic and unlearned (inborn) rewards like food and drink.

Primary sex characteristics.Definition: The reproductive organs (ovaries, uterus, and testes) and external genitals (vulva and penis).

Priming.Definition: Activating specific associations in memory either consciously or unconsciously.

Proactive interference.Definition: Occurs when something you learned earlier disrupts recall of something you experience later.

Problem solving.Definition: The active efforts we undertake to discover what must be done to achieve a goal that isn't readily attainable.

Procedural memory.Definition: Memories of perceptual, motor, and cognitive skills.

Projection.Definition: Freudian defense mechanism that attributes our undesirable feelings to others.

Projective personality tests.Definition: Present ambiguous stimuli such as inkblots (Rorschach) or pictures (TAT) with the assumption that test takers will project their unconscious thoughts or feelings onto the stimuli (according to psychoanalytic approach).

Prospective memory.Definition: Our memory to perform a planned action or remembering to perform that planned action.

Prototype.Definition: A mental image or “best example” that incorporates all the features you associate with a particular category.

Psychiatrist.Definition: Medical doctor and mental health professional who can prescribe medication or perform surgery.

Psychoactive drug.Definition: A chemical that can pass through the blood-brain barrier to alter perception, thinking, behavior, and mood.

Psychoanalysis.Definition: Freudian form of therapy involving free association, dream analysis, resistance, and transference aimed at providing the patient insight into his or her unconscious motivations and conflicts.

Psychoanalyst.Definition: A therapist who has taken specialized training in psychoanalysis generally after earning either an MD or a PhD.

Psychoanalytic/Psychodynamic approach.Definition: Psychological perspective concerned with how unconscious instincts, conflicts, motives, and defenses influence behavior.

Psychological dependence.Definition: Intense desire to achieve a drugged state in spite of adverse effects.

Psychology.Definition: The science of behavior and mental processes.

Psychometricians.Definition: Focus on methods for acquiring and analyzing psychological data; measure mental traits, abilities, and processes.

Psychopathology.Definition: A pattern of abnormality evidenced by emotions, behaviors, or thoughts inappropriate to the situation that lead to personal distress or the inability to achieve important goals.

Psychopharmacotherapy.Definition: The use of psychotropic drugs to treat mental disorders.

Psychophysics.Definition: Study of the relationship between physical energy and psychological experiences.

Psychosis.Definition: Reality distortion evidenced by highly disordered thought processes.

Psychosurgery.Definition: Any surgical technique in which neural pathways in the brain are cut in order to change behavior, including lobotomy.

Psychoticism.Definition: Eysenck's personality dimension that measures our level of tough-mindedness, how hostile, ruthless, and insensitive we are; as opposed to tender-mindedness, how friendly, empathetic, and cooperative we are.

Puberty.Definition: The early adolescent period marked by accelerated growth and onset of the ability to reproduce.

Punishment.Definition: An aversive consequence that follows a voluntary behavior, thereby decreasing the probability the behavior will be repeated.

Pupil.Definition: Small, adjustable opening in the iris of the eye that is smaller in bright light and larger in darkness.

Quasi-experiment.Definition: Research method similar to a controlled experiment but in which random assignment to groups is not possible. It can provide strong evidence suggesting cause and effect relationships.

Random assignment.Definition: Division of the sample into groups such that every individual has an equal chance of being put in any group or condition.

Random selection.Definition: Choosing of members of a population such that every individual has an equal chance of being chosen.

Range.Definition: The difference between the largest score and the smallest score (quick and dirty).

Rational emotive therapy (RET).Definition: Cognitive treatment developed by Ellis which is based on confronting irrational thoughts; change in irrational thinking will lead to a change in irrational behavior.

Rationalization.Definition: Freudian defense mechanism that provides socially acceptable reasons for our inappropriate behavior.

Reaction formation.Definition: Freudian defense mechanism involving acting in a manner exactly opposite to our true feelings.

Real self.Definition: According to Rogers, the positive and original organism we are before society imposes conditions of worth on us.

Reality principle.Definition: The manner in which the ego delays gratification and otherwise deals with the environment in a planned rational fashion (in Freudian theory).

Recessive gene.Definition: The gene that is hidden or not expressed when the genes for a trait are different.

Reciprocal determinism.Definition: The characteristics of the person, the person's behavior, and the environment all affect one another in two-way causal relationships (according to Bandura).

Reciprocity.Definition: Compliance technique used by groups; individuals feel obligated to go along with a request for a small donation if they have first accepted a small gift.

Recognition.Definition: Identification of learned items when they are presented.

Reconstruction.Definition: Retrieval of memories often distorted by adding, dropping, or changing details to fit a schema.

Reflex arc.Definition: The path over which the reflex travels that typically includes a receptor, sensory or afferent neuron, interneuron, motor or efferent neuron, and effector.

Regression.Definition: Freudian defense mechanism characterized by immature, pleasurable behavior of an earlier level of development.

Rehearsal.Definition: The conscious repetition of information to either maintain information in STM or to encode it for storage into long-term memory.

Reinforcer.Definition: In operant conditioning, any event that strengthens the behavior it follows.

Relearning.Definition: A measure of retention of memory that assesses the time saved compared to learning the first time when learning information again.

Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimula.Definition: A treatment for depression involving repeated pulses through a magnetic coil positioned above the right eyebrow of the patient that does not result in memory loss.

Replication.Definition: Repetition of the methods used in a previous experiment to see whether the same methods will yield the same results.

Representativeness heuristic.Definition: Tendency to judge the likelihood of things according to how they relate to a prototype; in social psychology the pre-judgment of people in the same way.

Repression.Definition: Most frequently used Freudian defense mechanism, characterized by unconscious forgetting; pushing threatening thoughts, feelings, and memories into the unconscious mind.

Resistance.Definition: Blocking of anxiety-provoking feelings and experiences in the process of psychoanalysis.

Resistance stage.Definition: Second stage of Selye's general adaptation syndrome characterized by the use of “fight or flight” mechanisms to control, cope with, or flee from the stressful situation.

Resistant attachment.Definition: Mixed reactions of infants to their mothers in the Strange Situation. They may approach their mothers upon their return but, at the same time, continue to cry or even push their mothers away.

Reticular formation.Definition: A network of neurons extending from the brainstem/hindbrain into the midbrain; essential to the regulation of sleep, wakefulness, arousal, and attention.

Retina.Definition: Light-sensitive surface in the back of the eye containing rods and cones that transduce light energy. Has layers of bipolar cells and ganglion cells that transmit visual information to the brain.

Retrieval.Definition: The process of getting information out of memory storage.

Retrieval cue.Definition: A stimulus that provides a trigger to get an item out of stored memory.

Retroactive inference.Definition: Recently learned information disrupts our ability to remember older information.

Retrograde amnesia.Definition: Involves memory loss for a segment of the past, usually around the time of an accident, such as a blow to the head.

Reversibility.Definition: Characteristic of Piaget's concrete operational stage, the logical negation of an operation, for example, if 4 + 2 = 6 then 6 - 2 = 4.

Rods.Definition: Photoreceptors that detect black, white, and gray and movement; are necessary for peripheral and dim-light vision when cones do not respond. Distributed throughout the retina of the eye, except in the fovea.

Roles.Definition: Ascribed social positions in groups and defined behavior expectations.

Rooting reflex.Definition: The newborn's tendency to move its head when stroked on the cheek, turn toward the stimulus as if searching for a nipple, and open its mouth.

Rorschach inkblot test.Definition: A projective test in which a person is shown a series of symmetrical inkblots and asked to describe what he or she thinks they represent.

Saltatory conduction.Definition: Rapid conduction of impulses when the axon is myelinated since depolarizations jump from node (of Ranvier) to node.

Sample.Definition: The subgroup of the population that participates in the study.

Savants.Definition: Individuals otherwise considered mentally retarded who have a specific exceptional skill typically in calculating, music, or art.

Scapegoat theory.Definition: Attributes prejudice to frustration; when own self-worth is in doubt or jeopardy, we find others to blame.

Schachter-Singer two-factor theory of em.Definition: An emotion is inferred from physiological arousal, and label of that emotion is based on our cognitive explanation for the arousal.

Schema.Definition: Framework of basic ideas and preconceptions about people, objects, and events based on past experience in long-term memory; concepts or frameworks that organize and interpret information.

Schizophrenia.Definition: A serious schizophrenic spectrum disorder characterized by thought disturbances, hallucinations, anxiety, emotional withdrawal, and delusions.

Seasonal affective disorder.Definition: A mood disorder characterized by depression, lethargy, sleep disturbances, and craving for carbohydrates; generally occurs during the winter, when the amount of daylight is low, and is sometimes treated with exposure to bright lights.

Second order conditioning.Definition: Learning procedure in which a well-learned conditioned stimulus is paired with a new neutral stimulus resulting in a similar conditioned response.

Secondary motive.Definition: Internal mechanism directing learned behavior as being desired, such as power and wealth.

Secondary reinforcer.Definition: Something seen as rewarding because it is associated with a primary reinforcer.

Secondary sex characteristics.Definition: The nonreproductive sexual characteristics including developed breasts in females; facial hair, Adam's apple, and deepened voice in males; and pubic hair and underarm hair in both.

Selective attention.Definition: Focusing of awareness on a specific stimulus (while excluding others) in sensory memory.

Self-actualization.Definition: The realization of our true intellectual and emotional potential (according to Maslow).

Self archetype.Definition: According to Jung, our sense of wholeness or unity.

Self-awareness.Definition: Consciousness of oneself as a person.

Self-concept.Definition: Our overall view of our abilities, behavior, and personality or what we know about ourselves.

Self-efficacy.Definition: How competent and able we feel to accomplish tasks; an expectation of success.

Self-esteem.Definition: How worthy we think we are.

Self-fulfilling prophecy.Definition: A tendency to let our preconceived expectations of others influence how we treat them and thus evoke those very expectations.

Self-referent encoding.Definition: Determining how new information relates to us personally.

Self-report methods.Definition: Most common personality assessment technique, involves person answering a series of questions such as a personality questionnaire or supplying information about himself or herself.

Self-serving bias.Definition: Our tendency to take personal credit for our achievements and blame failures on situational factors; to perceive ourselves favorably.

Semantic encoding.Definition: Information processed for meaning into short-term memory and long-term memory.

Semantic memories.Definition: A type of long-term memory that includes general knowledge, objective facts, and vocabulary.

Semantic networks.Definition: Model of long-term memory with more irregular and distorted systems than strict hierarchies, with multiple links from one concept to others.

Semantics.Definition: A set of rules we use to derive meaning from morphemes, words, and sentences.

Sensation.Definition: The process by which we detect physical energy from our environment and encode it as neural signals.

Sensorimotor stage.Definition: Piaget's first stage (0–2 years) during which the infant experiences the world through senses and action patterns; progresses from reflexes to object permanence and symbolic thinking.

Sensory adaptation.Definition: A temporary decrease in sensitivity to a stimulus that occurs when stimulation is unchanging.

Sensory memory.Definition: Primitive, brief type of memory that holds incoming information just long enough for further processing.

Sensory receptor.Definition: Cell typically in sense organs that initiates action potentials which then travel along sensory/afferent neurons to the CNS.

Separation anxiety.Definition: A set of fearful responses, such as crying, arousal, and clinging to the caregiver, that infants exhibit when the caregiver attempts to leave the infant.

Serial position effect.Definition: The tendency to remember and recall information that comes at the beginning (primacy effect) and at the end of a list of words (recency effect) more easily than those in the middle.

Serotonin.Definition: A neurotransmitter associated with arousal, sleep, appetite, moods, and emotions. A lack of serotonin is associated with depression.

Set point.Definition: A preset natural body weight, determined by the number of fat cells in our body.

Sex-linked traits.Definition: Recessive genes located on the X chromosome with no corresponding gene on the Y chromosome result in expression of recessive trait more frequently in males.

Sexual orientation.Definition: The direction of an individual's sexual interest.

Sexual response cycle.Definition: Masters and Johnson's four stages of bodily response during sex: excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution.

Shadow.Definition: According to Jung represents our baser instinctual urges we attempt to keep hidden from others.

Shallow processing.Definition: Encoding into memory superficial sensory information without making it relevant that seldom results in enduring memory.

Shaping.Definition: Positively reinforcing closer and closer approximations of a desired behavior through operant conditioning.

Short-term memory.Definition: Also called working memory, which can hold about seven unrelated items for about 20 to 30 seconds without rehearsal.

Simultaneous conditioning.Definition: In classical conditioning the CS and UCS are paired together at the same time; weaker conditioning technique than the ideal delayed conditioning.

Signal detection theory.Definition: Maintains that minimum threshold varies with fatigue, attention, expectations, motivation, and emotional distress, as well as from one person to another.

Single-blind procedure.Definition: Research design in which participants don't know whether they are in the experimental or control group.

Situational attributions.Definition: Inferences that a person's behavior is caused by some temporary condition or situation the person is in.

Sleep.Definition: A complex combination of states of consciousness each with its own level of consciousness, awareness, responsiveness, and physiological arousal.

Sleepwalking.Definition: Most frequently a childhood sleep disruption that occurs during NREM-3 sleep characterized by trips out of bed or carrying on of complex activities.

Social clock.Definition: Idea that society has certain age expectations for when someone should marry and have kids and people feel compelled to meet these expectations or face a crisis.

Social cognition.Definition: Refers to the way people gather, use, and interpret information about the social aspects of the world around them.

Social facilitation.Definition: Improved performance of well- learned tasks in front of others.

Social group.Definition: Two or more people sharing common goals and interests interact and influence behavior of the other(s).

Social impairment.Definition: Worsened performance of a newly learned or difficult task when performed in front of an audience.

Social interactivist perspective.Definition: Babies are biologically equipped for learning language, which may be activated or constrained by experience.

Social learning theory.Definition: Bandura's idea that we can learn behavior from others by first observing it and then imitating it.

Social loafing.Definition: The tendency of individuals to put less effort into group projects than when they are individually accountable.

Social motives.Definition: Learned needs that energize behavior; acquired as part of growing up in a particular society or culture.

Social psychologists.Definition: Psychologists who focus on how a person's mental life and behavior are shaped by interactions with other people.

Social psychology.Definition: The study of how groups influence the attitudes and behavior of the individual.

Social referencing.Definition: Observing the behavior of others in social situations to obtain information or guidance.

Social skills training.Definition: Cognitive behavioral therapy where the therapist can model the behavior for the client and then place the client in a simulated situation for practice.

Sociobiology.Definition: Study of the biological basis of social behavior.

Sociocultural approach.Definition: Psychological perspective concerned with how cultural differences affect behavior.

Somatic nervous system.Definition: Subdivision of PNS that includes motor nerves that stimulate skeletal (voluntary) muscle.

Somatic symptom disorder (SSD).Definition: Characterized by physical symptoms including pain and high anxiety in these individuals about having a disease. Patients need to have complained about, taken medicine for, changed lifestyle because of, or seen a physician about the symptoms and experienced anxiety that has interfered with carrying on normal activities for 6 months.

Somatosensation.Definition: The skin sensations: touch/pressure, warmth, cold, and pain.

Somatotype theory.Definition: William Sheldon's theory that body types determine personality.

Sound localization.Definition: The process by which you determine the location of a sound.

Source trait.Definition: Cattell's underlying 16 traits that guide your behavior.

Speed test.Definition: Measures how fast you can answer questions in a specified time period.

Spinal cord.Definition: Portion of the central nervous system below the medulla oblongata.

Split-half reliability.Definition: A method where the score on one half of the test questions is compared with the score on the other half of the questions to see if they are consistent.

Spontaneous recovery.Definition: The reappearance of a previously extinguished CR after a rest period.

Stability versus change.Definition: Deals with the issue of whether or not personality traits present during infancy persist throughout the lifespan.

Standard deviation (SD).Definition: A measure of the average difference between each score and the mean of the data set; the square root of the variance.

Standardization.Definition: Two-part test development procedure that first establishes test norms by giving the test to a large representative sample of those for whom the test is designed, and then ensures that the test is both administered and scored uniformly for all test takers.

Standardized tests.Definition: Set of tasks administered under standard conditions to assess an individual's knowledge, skill, or personality characteristics.

Stanford–Binet intelligence test.Definition: Terman's revision of Binet's original individual IQ test.

State-dependent memory.Definition: Tendency to recall information better if you are in the same internal state as when the information was encoded.

Statistical significance (p).Definition: Condition that exists when the probability that the observed findings are due to chance is less than 1 in 20 (p < .05) according to some psychologists or less than 1 in 100 (p < .01) according to those with more stringent standards.

Statistics.Definition: Field that involves the analysis of numerical data about representative samples of populations..

Stereotype.Definition: Overgeneralized belief about the characteristics of members of a particular group; schema used to quickly judge others.

Stereotype threat.Definition: Anxiety that influences members of a group concerned that their performance will confirm a negative stereotype.

Stimulants.Definition: Psychoactive drugs that activate motivational centers and reduce activity in inhibitory centers of the central nervous system by increasing activity of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine neurotransmitter systems; include caffeine, nicotine, amphetamines, and cocaine.

Stimulus.Definition: A change in the environment that can be detected by sensory receptors; elicits (brings about) a response.

Storage.Definition: The retention of encoded information over time.

Stranger anxiety.Definition: The fear of strangers that infants develop at around 8 months of age.

Stress.Definition: The process by which we appraise and respond to environmental threats.

Stressors.Definition: Stimuli such as heat, cold, pain, that are perceived as endangering our well-being.

Strive for superiority.Definition: According to Adler, this tendency is a result of a need to compensate for our feelings of inferiority.

Structuralism.Definition: Early psychological perspective that emphasized units of consciousness and identification of elements of thought using introspection.

Sublimation.Definition: Freudian defense mechanism, expression of sexual or aggressive impulses redirected into more socially acceptable behaviors.

Subliminal stimulation.Definition: Receiving messages below your absolute threshold for conscious awareness.

Sucking.Definition: The automatic response of drawing in anything at the mouth.

Sulci.Definition: Folding-in portions of convolutions of the cerebral cortex.

Superego.Definition: The third part of Freud's personality systems which makes us feel proud when we obey its strict morality and feel guilt when we give in to the id's more pleasure-seeking urges.

Superstitious behavior.Definition: Idiosyncratic, unimportant behavior associated with anticipation of a reward as a result of unintended reinforcement.

Surface trait.Definition: Cattell's cluster of personality traits which stems from deep source traits; the person we see on the outside.

Survey.Definition: Research method that obtains large samples of abilities, beliefs, or behaviors at a specific time and place through questionnaire or interview.

Swallowing.Definition: Automatic contraction of throat muscles that enables food to pass into the esophagus without our choking.

Sympathetic nervous system.Definition: Subdivision of PNS and ANS whose stimulation results in responses that help the body deal with stressful events.

Symptom substitution.Definition: The replacement of one behavior that has been eliminated with another.

Synapse.Definition: Region of communication between the transmitting presynaptic neuron and receiving postsynaptic neuron or muscle or gland, consisting of the presynaptic terminal buttons, a tiny space, and receptor sites typically on the postsynaptic dendrites.

Syntax.Definition: Rules that are used to order words into grammatically sensible sentences.

Systematic desensitization.Definition: Behavior treatment for phobias in which the client is trained to relax to increasingly fearful stimuli.

Tardive dyskinesia.Definition: Serious side effects from antipsychotic drugs including problems walking, drooling, and involuntary muscle spasms.

Taste aversion.Definition: Negative response to particular foods that may be inborn and/or acquired through classical conditioning.

Tay-Sachs syndrome.Definition: Recessive trait that produces progressive loss of nervous function and death in a baby.

Telegraphic speech.Definition: Meaningful two-word sentences, usually a noun and a verb, and usually in the correct order uttered by 2-year-olds.

Temperament.Definition: An infant's natural disposition to show a particular mood at a particular intensity for a specific period.

Temporal conditioning.Definition: In classical conditioning, the presentation of the UCS at specific periods; time serves as the CS.

Temporal lobes.Definition: Side regions of cerebral cortex that are primary areas for hearing, understanding language (Wernicke's area), understanding music/ tonality, and processing smell.

Teratogen.Definition: Harmful substance (drug or virus) with which contact during the prenatal period can cause birth defect(s).

Terminal buttons.Definition: Tips at the end of axons which secrete neurotransmitters when stimulated by the action potential.

Testes.Definition: Gonads in males that produce hormones necessary for reproduction and development of secondary sex characteristics.

Thalamus.Definition: Part of forebrain that relays visual, auditory, taste, somatosensory (skin sensation) information to and from appropriate areas of cerebral cortex; involved in encoding sensory memory into STM.

Thanatology.Definition: Study of death and dying; Kübler-Ross's five stages of facing death: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance.

Thematic Apperception Test (TAT).Definition: A projective test composed of ambiguous pictures about which a person is asked to write a complete story.

Theories.Definition: Organized sets of concepts that explain phenomena.

Thinking.Definition: Involves mental images, symbols, concepts, and rules of language.

Thyroid gland.Definition: Endocrine gland in neck that produces thyroxin, which stimulates and maintains metabolic activities.

Timbre.Definition: Te quality of a sound determined by the purity of a waveform; a note of the same pitch and loudness sounds different on different musical instruments.

Tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon.Definition: Retrieval problem that involves known information that can only be retrieved incompletely; better cues are required for retrieval.

Token economy.Definition: A program used in institutions in which a person's acceptable behavior is reinforced with tokens that can be exchanged for special privileges or goods.

Tolerance.Definition: Condition in which diminished effectiveness of drug necessitates larger dosages to produce desired effect.

Top-down processing.Definition: Information processing guided by preexisting knowledge or expectations to construct perceptions; concept-driven.

Trace conditioning.Definition: In classical conditioning, the CS is presented first, removed, and then the UCS is presented.

Trait.Definition: A relatively permanent and stable characteristic that can be used to predict behavior.

Transduction.Definition: Transformation of stimulus energy to the electrochemical energy of neural impulses.

Transference.Definition: In psychoanalysis, the venting of emotions both positive and negative by patients; treating their analyst as the symbolic representative of someone important in their past.

Triadic reciprocality model of personali.Definition: Bandura's scheme that our personal traits, the environment, and our behavior all interact to account for our behavior.

Trial and error.Definition: Trying possible solutions and discarding those that fail to solve the problem.

Triarchic theory of intelligence.Definition: Robert Sternberg's idea of three separate and testable intelligences: analytical (facts), practical (“street smarts”), creative (seeing multiple solutions).

Trichromatic theory.Definition: Proposed mechanism for color vision with cones that are differentially sensitive to different wavelengths of light; each color seen results from a specific ratio of activation among the three types of receptors.

Turner syndrome.Definition: A group of symptoms in females with only one X sex chromosome, including shortness, sterility, webbed neck, and difficulty with calculations.

Type A personalities.Definition: Hard-driving, competitive, impatient, and ambitious individuals.

Unconditional positive regard.Definition: Rogers's term for acceptance, value, and love from others independent of how we behave.

Unconditioned response (UCR).Definition: In classical conditioning, the unlearned, naturally occurring response (reaction) to the unconditioned stimulus.

Unconditioned stimulus (UCS).Definition: In classical conditioning, the stimulus (change) that naturally and automatically triggers the reflexive unconditioned response (UR).

Unconscious.Definition: The level of consciousness of which we are unaware, which may include unacceptable feelings, wishes, and thoughts not directly available to conscious awareness, according to psychodynamic psychologists/psychoanalysts. According to cognitive psychologists, the unconscious is the level of consciousness that parallel processes information of which we are unaware.

Unconsciousness.Definition: Characterized by loss of responsiveness to the environment resulting from disease, trauma, or anesthesia.

Undifferentiated schizophrenia.Definition: Simple schizophrenia characterized by fragments of the symptoms of other, different types of schizophrenia.

Uninvolved parenting style.Definition: Characterized by few demands, low responsiveness, little communication, and general detachment from a child's life.

Validity.Definition: The extent to which an instrument measures or predicts what it is supposed to.

Variability.Definition: The spread or dispersion of a set of research data or distribution.

Variable interval.Definition: Schedule of reinforcement in which responses are reinforced after varying lengths of time (in operant conditioning).

Variable ratio.Definition: Schedule of reinforcement in which reinforcement is presented after a varying number of responses (in operant conditioning).

Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH).Definition: Originally called the satiety center, or “off” button, for hunger. When stimulated, it turns off the urge to eat and when removed, the organism will continue to eat excessively and gain weight rapidly.

Vestibular sense.Definition: Body sense of equilibrium with hairlike receptors in semicircular canals and vestibular sac in the inner ear.

Visual capture.Definition: Dominance of vision when there is a conflict among senses.

Visual encoding.Definition: The encoding of pictorial images into our memory.

Weber's law.Definition: Difference thresholds increase in proportion to the size of the stimulus.

Wechsler intelligence tests.Definition: The most widely used measurement of intelligence; three age-related individual IQ tests (WPPSI, WISC, WAIS) that provide two scores, verbal and performance.

Wernicke's area.Definition: Region in left temporal lobe that plays role in understanding language and making meaningful sentences.

Withdrawal.Definition: Intense craving for a drug accompanied by effects opposite of those the drug usually induces.

Womb envy.Definition: Horney's counterpart to penis envy of Freudian theory; male's desire to procreate.

Yerkes–Dodson rule.Definition: For easy tasks, moderately high arousal is needed to do well; for difficult tasks, moderately low; and most average tasks, moderate level of arousal.

Zone of proximal development (ZPD).Definition: According to Vygotsky, the range between the level at which a child can solve a problem working alone with difficulty and the level at which a child can solve a problem with the assistance of adults or more-skilled children.

Zygote.Definition: A fertilized egg with the genetic instructions for a new individual normally contained in 46 chromosomes.
